newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts pare losses after late Wed sell off.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts pare losses after late Wed sell off.

text.p: UK gilts recovered well from the lows made in after-hours trading on Wednesday after the budget, but they were still 10/32 down on the official pit settlement price.
Overseas buyers came to the market's aid, lured in by the pound's renewed strength on hopes of higher interest rates.
"There has certainly been foreign buying of fixed income stocks on the back of the strength of sterling," one trader said.
"There was some buying overnight and more today. With sterling still at these levels the foreigners seem to be very content to buy."
The September gilt future ended the day down at 114-15 compared to the previous close of 114-25.
Nevertheless they did recover some 17/32 on the opening price, dictated by the after-hours sell off following Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's budget speech.
Many analysts said Brown did not go far enough in his budget to rein in consumer demand, and that the only thing left to control the economy is monetary policy.
"The only weapon left is interest rates to control the economy, and if they go up, sterling will go up in anticipation of it," the trader said.

Brown handed the over the power to set interest rates to the Bank of England in one of his first policy measures, leaving him to set the inflation targets. The Bank of England monetary policy committee meets to discuss rates next week with its decision coming on July 10.
Earlier in the day, buoyant June retail sales figures and a strong PMI services sector survey provided further justification for an early rate rise to dampen consumer demand.

"Because Brown did not exactly tighten policy on the consumers yesterday, the encouraging CBI figures suggest even more upper pressure on interest rates," said Mark Wall, an economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) said 58 percent of retailers reported increased sales volumes in June compared with last year while 19 percent said they were down.

The Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply (CIPS) said the services sector grew at a slightly slower pace in June. The PMI business activity index slipped to a seasonally adjusted 62.9 from 64.2 in May but this was still the third highest reading since the survey began a year ago.
"We predict that the CBI and other surveys are going to look quite robust in the coming months," Wall said.
